chunks: "The standard circuit is a pushbutton from the GPIO pin to ground, with a pull-up resistor from the pin to 3. 3 volts.
When the button is open the pull-up holds the pin high, a logic 1. When it's pressed, the pin is shorted to ground, a logic 0. So the button is active-low.
A 10 kilohms pull-up is typical, which draws only 0. 33 milliamps, and only while the button is held.
Many MCUs have an internal pull-up I can enable, so the external resistor can be dropped.
The reason for the pull-up is that without it the pin would float when the button is open and read random values. Then the real-world issue is bounce.
A mechanical button chatters for a few milliseconds when pressed, so the MCU might see ten edges.

I can fix that in hardware with a capacitor, say 100 nanofarads to 1 microfarads, across the switch, forming an RC with the pull-up, into a Schmitt-trigger input; or in software by sampling every millisecond and accepting a state only after it's been stable for about 20 milliseconds.
For firmware, either poll it from a timer tick, or use a pin interrupt on the falling edge if I want to wake from sleep, with a debounce timer so I don't get repeated interrupts.
If the button is on a front panel I'd add a series resistor, maybe 1 kilohms, for ESD and current limiting."
